AM4F-01.note: 5(-2)-(-2)^2 = -10-4 = -14. 14 is the whole-expression sign flip, -6 is (-10)+4 (squaring the negative wrong), 6 the combination of both. Options are two sign-pairs, so nothing singles out the key blind.

AM4F-02.note: f(2)=9, g(9)=5. The intermediate 9 is ON the ballot as a distractor, as is g(2)=-2 and the reversed composition f(g(2))=-7. Minor blind relation: -2 = 5 + (-7), but that flags a distractor, not the key.

AM4F-03.note: (x+9)/2 = 4 gives x = -1. 6.5 = h(4) for the student who never inverts; 17 = 2(4)+9 for the student who inverts by swapping in the wrong order; -5 = 4-9. Nothing reachable from the option set.

AM4F-04.note: 5d = 7-22 = -15, d = -3. -15 (the total change over five gaps) is the intended trap and it is genuine. 3 is the sign flip. 4 corresponds to no error I can name — closest is miscounting gaps as 5 into 22-7, which still does not give 4; that one is weak. Blind: -3/3 is a sign pair, mild.

AM4F-05.note: cos ranges [-1,1], -4cos is [-4,4], max = 4+5 = 9. 1 is the minimum, a real error. 17 needs the student to read the inside 3 as the amplitude (-4(-3)+5); reachable but strained. 12 corresponds to no error — 4x3 is not a step anyone takes here. Weak third option.

AM4F-06.note: SYMBOLIC. Right 3 is x-3, down 2 is -2. Option set alone narrows NOTHING: a perfectly balanced 2x2 over (x-3 / x+3) x (+2 / -2), each sign error represented exactly once. This is the shape the other symbolic items should be measured against.

AM4F-07.note: 2x+7 = 0. Options are the full sign-x-reciprocal cross of 7/2, so blind the set is exactly balanced and gives nothing. The zero of the numerator (x=1) is deliberately not on the ballot, which is fine since it is not among the four shapes.

AM4F-08.note: RE-KEYED ITEM. a5 = a2*r^3, so r^3 = (5/3)/45 = 1/27. Asking for r^3 reads acceptably — sequence items do ask for a ratio power — but it costs the item its last step, and r = 1/3 sitting as a distractor means the only students who miss it are the ones who did the EXTRA work of taking the cube root. The re-key made the item easier and inverted who gets it wrong. Option set is a balanced sign/reciprocal cross; no blind narrowing.

AM4F-09.note: SYMBOLIC. Balanced 2x2 over base {3,8} x divisor {3,8}; the option set alone narrows nothing structurally. The only route in without modelling is content knowledge (3 is the factor, 8 the period), which is what the item is testing.

AM4F-10.note: RE-KEYED ITEM, and the one that reads most naturally of the four. f(4)-f(1) = 48-(-3) = 51. Asking for total change is standard ACT phrasing; nothing about the stem betrays the repair. 48 = f(4), the intermediate, now correctly a distractor; 63 = 4^3-1^3 (differencing the cubes only). 17 corresponds to no error I can reconstruct — weak.

AM4F-11.note: 1 < 3 so f(1) = 8; 8 >= 3 so f(8) = 60. 8 (the intermediate) and 22 = 2(8)+6 (staying in the wrong branch) and 0 = 2(-3)+6 (entering the wrong branch first) are all endpoints of real branch errors. Good item.

AM4F-12.note: Axis at x = 3, so k = 2(3)-1 = 5. 3 is the vertex x itself (the classic stop-one-step-early); -1 and -5 are sign handlings of the reflection. The stem's 'other than 1' clause is load-bearing and 1 is correctly NOT on the ballot, so the clause is not decorative here — it names the excluded root rather than selecting among two on the ballot.

AM4F-13.note: sqrt(3x+4) = 7, 3x+4 = 49, x = 15. 7 is the intermediate radical value (distractor, correctly); 0 comes from squaring the 2 instead of the 7; 5/3 from 3x+4=9. No extraneous root to worry about — 15 checks.

AM4F-14.note: SYMBOLIC. x = -b/2a = -3, y = 9-18-1 = -10. Option set alone: balanced 2x2 over (-3 / 3) x (-10 / 8) — no narrowing from the set. A testwise student narrows to the -10 pair by knowing an upward parabola's vertex is its minimum, but that is content, not a structural tell. Both coordinates must be computed to choose, which is what keeps it out of easy.

AM4F-15.note: Leading coefficients 6/2 = 3. 1/3 is the inverted ratio, 0 the student who thinks the denominator always wins, 6/5 the ratio of the numerator's own coefficients. All three are errors people make.

AM4F-16.note: 3^2 = x+5, x = 4. 14 = 9+5 (sign on the shift) is strong. 1 and 20 are filler — 1 might be 3(2)-5 and 20 has no derivation I can name. Two weak options in a four-choice set means this item is close to a two-way guess for a student who knows only the log-to-exponent move.

AM4F-17.note: f(-2) = -2, g(-2) = -12, difference = 10. -2 is the intermediate f(-2) (distractor); -14 is f+g instead of f-g; -10 is 5(-2) for the student who drops g's constant. The double negative is the whole difficulty and it is a slip, not a reasoning step.

AM4F-18.note: RE-KEYED ITEM, and it READS FORCED. 3h25m = first hour ($5) plus 2h25m billed as three additional blocks ($9); total $14. The natural stem here is 'what is the total charge', and 'How many dollars of the total charge are for the time after the first hour' is a clause that exists to move the key off 14 — it is the second most audibly re-keyed stem in the batch. The mathematics is unharmed and 14 is now a strong distractor, but 6 (two blocks) is the only error the re-key still catches, so the item now tests the ceiling rule once instead of twice.

AM4F-19.note: RE-KEYED ITEM, and the MOST forced of the four. y = kx/z^2, 15 = 12k/4, k = 5. The stem has to narrate the solution method — 'a student first finds the constant of variation' — to justify stopping there, and ACT stems do not describe a student's procedure. It also strands the real answer (y = 1.875) as a distractor, which is a strong distractor but an odd one: the student who finishes the problem is punished for finishing. 2.5 (z not squared) and 45 are genuine. Consider restoring 'what is y when x=6 and z=4' and breaking the intermediate relation another way.

AM4F-20.note: Minimum = 11 - b^2/4 = 2, so b^2 = 36 and b = -6 by the stated sign. The disambiguating clause IS doing work and 6 is correctly ON the ballot — this is the item the protocol's inverse test wants to see. Partial blind leak: 'b is a negative constant' halves the set to {-6, -3} before any work, but -3 and 3 are the genuine b/2 confusion, so the leak is a cost of honest distractors, not a defect.

AM4F-21.note: h(x) = 2(x/4+3)-1 = x/2+5; x/2+5 = 9 gives x = 8. 9.5 = h(9) (forward instead of inverse) is the main trap; 5 and 12.5 come from composing in the wrong order or inverting only one piece. Two chained ideas, but neither is hard — medium, not hard.

AM4F-22.note: Checked t = 12: 12,590.85 vs 12,900 (A still behind by 309). t = 13: 13,598 vs 12,900. Key 13. The t=12 near-miss is an excellent distractor — the margin is 2.4%, so a student who estimates rather than computes takes it. 8 is where A passes the 9,000 intercept alone, also real. 41 is the endpoint of no error and reads as a fourth option needed to fill the slot. Genuinely hard for the time budget: this is guess-and-check on a calculator.

AM4F-23.note: SYMBOLIC. Need 1/(x-6) - 2 >= 0 with x != 6. x > 6 forces 1 >= 2(x-6), x <= 6.5; x < 6 makes the reciprocal negative and fails. So 6 is open (undefined) and 6.5 is closed (radicand 0). Option set alone narrows NOTHING — all four endpoint combinations are present and balanced, which is exactly right, and every one of the three wrong ones is the endpoint of a real slip (forgetting the domain of g, or barring the zero radicand). Hardest item in the batch and the best-constructed.

AM4F-24.note: 3x-9 = +/-15 gives x = 8 or x = -2. The superlative is doing real work and -2 is correctly ON the ballot. Note the superlative does NOT hand over the key: 24 is the largest-valued option, so 'pick the biggest number' fails, which is the right way to build this. 2 = (15-9)/3 is a genuine slip.

AM4F-25.note: 12/(1-r) = 20, 1-r = 3/5, r = 2/5. 3/5 is (1-r), the intermediate and the single most common wrong answer on this item type. -2/5 and -2/3 are sign handlings. Clean.

AM4F-26.note: SYMBOLIC, and the ONE symbolic item whose option set narrows. Factor to (x-5)(x+2)/(x-5) = x+2 with a hole at x = 5, y = 7. But the four options are (5,3), (-2,7), (-2,0), (5,7): x = 5 twice, x = -2 twice, and y = 7 TWICE against 3 and 0 once each. Taking the modal y cuts the set from four to two without any algebra, and the key is in that pair. Not enough for exclusive false — it is still a coin flip from there — but it is a free 50% and the other four symbolic items do not give it. Fix by making the y-values distinct. (-2,0) is the genuine root confusion; (5,3) corresponds to no error.

AM4F-27.note: 5 -> 7 -> 11 -> 19. 11 = a(3) and 37 = a(5) are the two off-by-one stopping points, which is the correct distractor family for a recursion. -2 is filler. Three iterations of one-line arithmetic; easy.

AM4F-28.note: 240 * (1/2)^(15/6) = 240 * 2^-2.5 = 42.43, rounds to 42. 60 = 240/4 is the student who takes floor(15/6) = 2 halvings and is strong. 96 and 182 I cannot trace to a step — 182 is roughly one-and-a-bit halvings, 96 is 240 x 0.4. Two of three distractors are unmotivated. The non-integer exponent is what makes this medium rather than easy.
